mainTopic: Shabbat 50b: Washing substances on שבת and beautifying oneself, then the pot in the basket and pulling objects out of earth or bricks on שבת.
overview: The גמרא first finishes explaining two conflicting ברייתות about cleaning with sand and נתר. It concludes that both follow רבי יהודה and that they only disagree about whether these substances scrape. The permission to wash the face is explained as referring to someone with no beard. Next, several אמוראים list substances that anyone may use to wash on שבת, including ברדא, which is defined as a herbal mixture without a majority of אהלא. רב ששת forbids splitting olives for their oil even on a weekday, because it makes food disgusting, and the גמרא shows this does not contradict שמואל's ruling about bread. A story about אמימר, רב אשי and מר זוטרא shows two views on beautifying oneself, each based on a ברייתא. The גמרא then returns to the משנה of the pot in the basket and explains that everyone forbids returning the pot once the hole collapsed. The argument is only about worrying that it might collapse. Related rules follow about pulling a branch or knife out of earth, bricks or reeds on שבת. A strong challenge to these rules from a משנה about a buried turnip begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי שמעון allows a נזיר to wash his hair
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites רבי שמעון's ruling that a נזיר may wash and separate his hair but may not comb it. This shows that רבי שמעון permits washing even where pulling out hair is forbidden, which undercuts the earlier attempt to assign one ברייתא to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A נזיר may wash his hair and separate it with his fingers, but he may not comb it!
steps.whatsHappening: This amud starts mid-argument. The גמרא quotes רבי שמעון's rule about a נזיר to show that the earlier way of splitting the ברייתות between רבי שמעון and רבי יהודה does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נזיר is forbidden to remove hair, yet רבי שמעון still lets him wash it, since any hair that falls out is unintended (דבר שאין מתכוין). Combing is different because it is certain to pull out hair. So רבי שמעון does not forbid washing just because hair might fall out, and the attribution built on him falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: A person under a vow who may not cut or remove hair
Separates the hair with the fingers

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a brand-new topic about נזירות. It is a source being quoted to attack the previous explanation of the ברייתות.

phrases.english: A nazirite may wash and separate [his hair],
phrases.notes: Washing might pull out hair, but that is unintended.

phrases.english: but he may not comb it!
phrases.notes: Combing will certainly pull out hair (פסיק רישיה).

steps.triggerLanguage: נָזִיר חוֹפֵף וּמְפַסְפֵּס, אֲבָל לֹא סוֹרֵק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion (on the previous amud) that assigned the two ברייתות to רבי שמעון and רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier explanation that one ברייתא follows רבי שמעון and the other follows רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי שמעון permits washing even where hair removal is forbidden, so the split between the two תנאים does not fit.

steps.title: Both ברייתות follow רבי יהודה, with two views of his position
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the earlier split and says both ברייתות follow רבי יהודה. Two תנאים disagree about whether sand and נתר scrape the vessel.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, both this ברייתא and that ברייתא follow רבי יהודה, and there are two תנאים who hold like רבי יהודה. One holds that sand and נתר scrape the vessel, so it is forbidden. The other holds they do not scrape, so it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: Using the word אלא ("rather"), the גמרא offers a completely new way to resolve the two conflicting ברייתות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides now agree with רבי יהודה that unintended acts are forbidden. The disagreement is moved from a principle (דבר שאין מתכוין) to a factual question: does sand or נתר actually scrape and smooth the silver? Whoever says it scrapes forbids it, and whoever says it does not, permits it.

keyTerms.meaning: This one and that one (both sources)
Two תנאים disagreeing about what a given authority holds

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common גמרא move: a disagreement between ברייתות can be about facts (does it scrape?) rather than about a legal principle.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא הָא וְהָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא,
phrases.english: Rather, both this and that are Rabbi Yehuda,
phrases.notes: Both ברייתות hold that an unintended act is forbidden.

phrases.english: and there are two tanna'im according to Rabbi Yehuda.
This tanna, according to Rabbi Yehuda,
holds that it scrapes,
phrases.notes: So it is forbidden on שבת.

phrases.english: and that tanna, according to Rabbi Yehuda,
holds that it does not scrape.
phrases.notes: So it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָא וְהָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the explanation that was undermined in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning both sources to one authority, with a factual dispute about his view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתות were thought to disagree because one followed רבי שמעון and the other followed רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both follow רבי יהודה. They differ only on whether sand and נתר scrape (גריר).

steps.title: Challenge: the end of the ברייתא permits washing the face
steps.stepSummary: If the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, why does its end permit washing the face, hands, and feet with sand and נתר? That should cause hair to fall out, which רבי יהודה forbids even when unintended.
steps.simpleTranslation: How did you explain the ברייתא? As following רבי יהודה. Then look at the end of it: "But his face, hands, and feet are permitted." Doesn't that remove hair?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new explanation from step 2 by pointing to the last clause (סיפא) of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה forbids unintended acts, so any washing that might pull out hair should be forbidden in his view. Yet the סיפא openly permits washing the face, which has hair. That clash makes it look like the ברייתא cannot follow רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: How did you establish it? According to Rabbi Yehuda,
then say the latter clause:
But his face, his hands, and his feet are permitted.
phrases.notes: That is, to wash with sand and נתר.

phrases.english: But this removes hair!
phrases.notes: So it should be forbidden according to רבי יהודה.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי אוֹקֵימְתָּא כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new explanation given in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה forbids unintended hair removal, yet the סיפא permits washing the face, which would remove hair.

steps.title: The face case is someone without facial hair
steps.stepSummary: The permission to wash the face refers to someone with no facial hair (a קטן, an אשה, or a סריס), so there is no hair to remove.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say it is talking about a child. If you want, say a woman. If you want, say a סריס.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case in the סיפא to people who have no beard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the person has no facial hair, washing the face cannot pull any out. So the ברייתא can still follow רבי יהודה. The three options are interchangeable examples of the same idea.
steps.whatToRemember: Both ברייתות follow רבי יהודה, and their dispute is whether sand and נתר scrape. The permission to wash the face refers to a person without facial hair, so there is no unintended hair removal.
steps.confusionAlert: The three answers are not a disagreement. They are three examples of the same point: no facial hair means no problem.

phrases.english: If you wish, say it refers to a child,
and if you wish, say a woman,
and if you wish, say a eunuch.
phrases.notes: None of them has facial hair.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא בְּקָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge raised in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to people without facial hair
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The סיפא seemed to permit washing a bearded face, which would remove hair.
steps.terutzMaskana: The סיפא refers to someone with no beard, so it fits רבי יהודה.

steps.title: Four substances permitted for washing
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, רב יוסף, רבא and רב ששת each name a substance that may be used for washing on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: powder of לבינתא is permitted. רב יוסף said: the pressed leftovers of jasmine are permitted. רבא said: ground pepper is permitted. רב ששת said: ברדא is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now lists substances that are safe for washing on שבת, even for someone with a beard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps worried that sand and נתר pull out hair, so they were permitted only for someone with no facial hair. These four substances do not remove hair, so anyone may use them on שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: Powder of לבינתא (רש״י: crushed brick; רב האי גאון: frankincense)
The leftover pulp of jasmine after its oil is pressed out

steps.whyThisMatters: It gives practical options for washing on שבת without the hair-removal problem.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: עֲפַר לְבֵינְתָּא שְׁרֵי.
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: powder of livinta is permitted.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: כּוּסְפָּא דְיַסְמִין שְׁרֵי.
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: pressed jasmine residue is permitted.
Rava said: ground pepper is permitted.
Rav Sheshet said: berada is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: עֲפַר לְבֵינְתָּא שְׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After limiting sand and נתר to people with no facial hair, the גמרא lists substances that anyone may use.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Powder of לבינתא, jasmine residue, ground pepper and ברדא may be used for washing on שבת.

steps.title: What is ברדא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what ברדא is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is ברדא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask what the unfamiliar word ברדא means. This sets up the definition in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת permitted ברדא, but we cannot apply his ruling without knowing what the mixture contains.

keyTerms.meaning: A cleansing mixture used for washing

phrases.english: What is berada?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בַּרְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a term used by רב ששת in the previous step.

steps.title: ברדא is three equal parts
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף defines ברדא as one-third אהלא, one-third myrtle and one-third violets.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: one-third אהלא, one-third myrtle (אסא) and one-third violets.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the question by listing the three equal ingredients of ברדא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ברדא is a mixture of three plants, each one-third of the total. This tells us exactly what רב ששת permitted.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
one-third aloe and one-third myrtle
and one-third violets.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: תִּילְּתָא אַהֲלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of what ברדא is.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ברדא is equal thirds of אהלא, myrtle and violets.

steps.title: Any mix without a majority of aloe is fine
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמיה בר יוסף says that as long as אהלא is not the majority, the mixture is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמיה בר יוסף said: whenever there is no majority of אהלא, it is fine to use.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמיה בר יוסף adds that the parts do not need to be exactly one-third each. What matters is that אהלא is not more than half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's equal thirds is not a strict recipe. The concern is the אהלא, which can remove hair if it is the main part. So the mixture is permitted even if it has more than a third of אהלא, as long as it is less than a majority.

keyTerms.meaning: It is fine, it is permitted

steps.whatToRemember: ברדא is permitted as long as אהלא does not make up most of the mixture.

phrases.english: Rav Nechemya bar Yosef said:
anywhere that there is no majority of aloe —
it is fine.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל הֵיכָא דְּלֵיכָּא רוּבָּא אַהֲלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds flexibility to רב יוסף's equal-thirds definition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A mixture is permitted as long as אהלא is less than a majority.

steps.title: May one split olives on שבת?
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת is asked whether one may split olives on שבת, so that their oil can be used for washing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב ששת: may one split olives on שבת?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question about washing is brought to רב ששת. It asks whether one may crush olives to wash with the oil that comes out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the theme of what may be used for washing on שבת. Now the substance is olive oil squeezed out by splitting the olives.

phrases.english: They asked Rav Sheshet:
What is the law about splitting olives on Shabbat?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעוֹ מִינֵּיהּ מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from permitted washing powders to a new washing method, using olive oil.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether splitting olives to use their oil for washing is allowed on שבת.

steps.title: Forbidden even on a weekday because it ruins food
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that this is not allowed even on a weekday, because it wastes food.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: and did they permit it on a weekday? He holds it is forbidden because it ruins food.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers with a question: if this is not even allowed on a weekday, how could it be allowed on שבת? The גמרא then explains his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem has nothing to do with שבת. Splitting olives this way makes them unfit to eat, and ruining food is forbidden. So it is forbidden every day of the week.
steps.confusionAlert: רב ששת is not saying that splitting olives is a שבת prohibition. The problem is wasting food, which applies on weekdays too.

phrases.english: He said to them:
And did they permit it on a weekday?
He holds it is forbidden because of ruining food.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי בְּחוֹל מִי הִתִּירוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about splitting olives.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It is forbidden even on a weekday, because it ruins food.

steps.title: Does this contradict שמואל on using bread?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רב ששת argues with שמואל, who allows a person to use bread for all his needs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this argues with שמואל? For שמואל said: a person may do all his needs with bread!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב ששת by comparing his ruling to a statement of שמואל, which seems to allow using food in a way that spoils it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל lets a person use bread for any purpose, such as wiping, even though this spoils it. That suggests that spoiling food is not a concern, which would contradict רב ששת's reason.

phrases.english: Shall we say it argues with Shmuel,
for Shmuel said:
a person may do all his needs with bread!

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא פְּלִיגָא דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason רב ששת gave in the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's reason that splitting olives is forbidden because it ruins food.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל allows using bread for any need even though it spoils the bread. So spoiling food should not be a reason to forbid something.

steps.title: Bread stays edible, split olives become disgusting
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that bread used this way does not become disgusting, but split olives do.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: bread does not become disgusting, but these olives do become disgusting.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב ששת and שמואל do not argue. The two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bread used for a need can still be eaten afterward, so nothing is wasted. Split olives become disgusting and nobody will eat them, so that is true waste of food. Both rulings stand.
steps.whatToRemember: Using food is allowed if it stays edible, like bread. Making food disgusting and unfit to eat, like split olives, is forbidden waste.

phrases.english: They said:
bread does not become disgusting,
these olives do become disgusting.

steps.triggerLanguage: פַּת לָא מְאִיסָא, הָנֵי מְאִיסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by showing that the two cases are different.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב ששת seemed to argue with שמואל about whether using food in a way that affects it is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: They agree. Bread stays edible, so using it is fine. Split olives become disgusting, so splitting them is forbidden waste.

steps.title: Three sages are offered a washing mixture
steps.stepSummary: אמימר, מר זוטרא and רב אשי are sitting together and are brought בַּרְדָּא. Two of them wash with it, but מר זוטרא does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר, מר זוטרא and רב אשי were sitting together, and בַּרְדָּא was brought before them. אמימר and רב אשי washed with it. מר זוטרא did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that tests רב ששת's ruling that washing with בַּרְדָּא is allowed on שבת. This story sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two sages act on רב ששת's permission. מר זוטרא refuses, and his refusal looks like a disagreement with רב ששת. The next steps will explain why he refused.

keyTerms.meaning: A cleansing mixture made of herbs, used for washing

phrases.aramaic: אַמֵּימָר וּמָר זוּטְרָא וְרַב אָשֵׁי הֲווֹ יָתְבִי,
phrases.english: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting,
they brought berada before them.
phrases.notes: בַּרְדָּא is a cleansing mixture used for washing.

phrases.english: Ameimar and Rav Ashi washed,
Mar Zutra did not wash.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר וּמָר זוּטְרָא וְרַב אָשֵׁי הֲווֹ יָתְבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion of רב ששת's rulings about washing, now told through a story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, אמימר and רב אשי used בַּרְדָּא on שבת, but מר זוטרא did not.

steps.title: Why didn't מר זוטרא follow רב ששת?
steps.stepSummary: The other sages ask מר זוטרא whether he disagrees with רב ששת, who allowed בַּרְדָּא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Doesn't the Master agree with what רב ששת said, that בַּרְדָּא is allowed?
steps.whatsHappening: The other sages challenge מר זוטרא. They want to know why he refused something that רב ששת allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their assumption is that the only possible reason to refuse is a concern about שבת. If so, מר זוטרא is going against רב ששת's clear ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Doesn't the Master hold this view?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: לָא סָבַר לַהּ מָר
phrases.english: They said to him: Doesn't the Master hold
like that which Rav Sheshet said:
berada is permitted?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: לָא סָבַר לַהּ מָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the behavior of מר זוטרא described in the story.
steps.kashyaTarget: מר זוטרא's refusal to wash with בַּרְדָּא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב ששת allowed בַּרְדָּא on שבת, so refusing it seems to contradict an accepted ruling.

steps.title: מר זוטרא avoids it even on weekdays
steps.stepSummary: רב מרדכי explains that מר זוטרא's refusal has nothing to do with שבת. He does not use בַּרְדָּא even on a weekday.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרדכי said to them: Leave the Master out of this. He does not hold it is allowed even on a weekday.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרדכי answers the challenge. מר זוטרא's refusal is not about שבת at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed the issue was a שבת law. רב מרדכי shows that מר זוטרא has a weekday objection to this kind of washing. So he does not disagree with רב ששת about שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: Except for the Master, meaning: don't learn anything from him here

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think מר זוטרא is stricter about שבת. His concern is not a שבת concern at all. It applies every day of the week.

phrases.english: Rav Mordekhai said to them:
Except for the Master,

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲפִילּוּ בְּחוֹל נָמֵי לָא סְבִירָא לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: for even on a weekday he does not hold it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב מָרְדֳּכַי: בַּר מִינֵּיהּ דְּמָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing the reason: the refusal is not about שבת
steps.terutzHavaAmina: מר זוטרא disagrees with רב ששת about using בַּרְדָּא on שבת.
steps.terutzMaskana: מר זוטרא avoids בַּרְדָּא every day, so there is no disagreement with רב ששת's שבת ruling.

steps.title: The source for Mar Zutra's view
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא follows a ברייתא. It says a person may scrape off scabs to relieve pain, but may not do it just to look nicer.
steps.simpleTranslation: He follows what was taught in a ברייתא: A person may scrape off dried dirt crusts and scabs from his skin because they hurt him. But if he does it to make himself look nice, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the ברייתא that supports מר זוטרא. It explains why he does not use בַּרְדָּא even during the week.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא draws a line between removing something because of pain, which is allowed, and doing it to beautify oneself, which is forbidden. Washing with בַּרְדָּא is for beauty, so מר זוטרא avoids it every day.

keyTerms.meaning: Crusts of dried dirt or filth

phrases.english: He holds like that which was taught in a baraita:
A person may scrape off crusts of filth
and scabs of a wound that are on his flesh
because of his pain;
if it is in order to beautify, it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבַר לַהּ כִּי הָא דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind רב מרדכי's explanation.
steps.raayaObject: מר זוטרא's view that beautifying oneself is forbidden even on a weekday
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא that allows scraping because of pain but forbids it for beauty

steps.title: What is the source for the other two sages?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which opinion אמימר and רב אשי follow when they allow washing with בַּרְדָּא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they, whose opinion do they follow?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks about the other side. This question sets up the next step, which gives the source for אמימר and רב אשי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We now know מר זוטרא's source. To be fair to both sides, the גמרא looks for a ברייתא that would allow beautifying oneself.

phrases.english: And they, like whom do they hold?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִינְהוּ כְּמַאן סַבְרוּהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from מר זוטרא's source to the source of the other two sages.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that allows אמימר and רב אשי to beautify themselves with בַּרְדָּא

steps.title: Washing every day in honor of the Creator
steps.stepSummary: אמימר and רב אשי follow a ברייתא that says a person washes his face, hands and feet every day in honor of his Maker.
steps.simpleTranslation: They follow what was taught in a ברייתא: A person washes his face, hands and feet every day for the sake of his Maker, as it says: 'ה׳ made everything for His sake.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. It gives the ברייתא that supports washing and cleaning oneself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא sees caring for one's appearance as honoring ה׳, who created a beautiful world. This is the opposite of the ברייתא behind מר זוטרא. It explains why אמימר and רב אשי used בַּרְדָּא.

keyTerms.meaning: ה׳ made everything for His own sake (משלי ט״ז:ד׳)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two views about beautifying oneself. מר זוטרא forbids it even on weekdays, based on one ברייתא. אמימר and רב אשי allow it, and see it as honoring ה׳, based on another ברייתא.

phrases.english: Like that which was taught in a baraita:
A person washes his face, his hands and his feet
every day for the sake of his Maker,
because it is said:
"The Lord made everything for His sake."

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּתַנְיָא: רוֹחֵץ אָדָם פָּנָיו יָדָיו וְרַגְלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They follow the ברייתא that a person washes every day in honor of his Maker.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: tilting the basket
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה. רבי אלעזר בן עזריה says that if a pot is in a basket, one tilts the basket to its side to take the pot out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה says: With a basket, he tilts it on its side and takes the pot, because otherwise he might lift it out and the hole might collapse, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and quotes רבי אלעזר בן עזריה. This quote sets up רב's statement in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pot is insulated in a basket filled with wool. If he lifts it straight up, the wool may fall into the hole, and he cannot move the wool back on שבת. Tilting the basket keeps the hole open so the pot can be returned.

keyTerms.meaning: He tilts it on its side

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says:
A basket: he tilts it on its side and takes the pot,
lest he take it out, etc.
phrases.notes: Lest the wool collapse into the hole and he will be unable to return the pot.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה אוֹמֵר: קוּפָּה, מַטָּהּ עַל צִדָּהּ וְנוֹטֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the washing discussion and returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, one tilts the basket so the hole stays open.

steps.title: Everyone agrees: a collapsed hole means no returning
steps.stepSummary: רב says that even the חכמים, who disagree with רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, agree that if the hole collapsed, the pot may not be returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said that רבי חייא בר אשי said that רב said: Everyone agrees that if the hole was ruined, it is forbidden to put the pot back.
steps.whatsHappening: רב marks out a case where the two sides of the משנה do not argue. If the hole has already collapsed, nobody allows putting the pot back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים let a person lift the pot without tilting the basket and then return it. Still, they agree that once the hole has collapsed, returning the pot would mean pushing aside the wool, which is not allowed. Their argument is only about the worry that the hole might collapse, not about what to do once it already has.

keyTerms.meaning: The hole or cavity where the pot sat

steps.whyThisMatters: This statement shows exactly where the argument in the משנה lies. It is only about whether we fear the hole will collapse. In the case where it has already collapsed, both sides agree.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said that Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Ashi said that Rav said:
Everyone agrees
that if the hole was ruined,
that it is forbidden to put it back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב: הַכֹּל מוֹדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the משנה just quoted by pointing to a case where both sides agree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the hole in the wool collapsed, everyone, even the חכמים, forbids putting the pot back.

steps.title: Challenge to רב from the Sages' ruling in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites the חכמים in the משנה, who allow taking the pot out and putting it back. It argues this must mean they allow it even when the hole was ruined, which goes against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: the חכמים say a person may take the pot out and put it back. What is the case? If the hole was not ruined, the חכמים are obviously right, so why would anyone argue? Rather, it must be that they allow it even though the hole was ruined.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a challenge against רב. רב said that even the חכמים forbid putting the pot back if the hole collapsed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument works by testing both possible cases. If the hole is still fine, putting the pot back is so clearly allowed that רבי אלעזר בן עזריה would have no reason to argue. So the real argument must be about a ruined hole, and the חכמים allow it even then, which contradicts רב.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What case is this?
Hole, cavity (here, the hole the pot sits in)

steps.confusionAlert: "שַׁפִּיר קָא אָמְרִי רַבָּנַן" is not praise for the חכמים. It means their view would be so obvious in that case that no argument would make sense.

phrases.english: We learned: And the Sages say:
He takes it out and puts it back.
What is the case?
If the hole was not ruined,
phrases.notes: The hole in the basket's insulating material is still intact.

phrases.english: then the Rabbis are obviously right.
phrases.notes: So why would רבי אלעזר בן עזריה argue?

phrases.english: Rather, is it not
even though the hole was ruined?

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן, וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: נוֹטֵל וּמַחֲזִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's statement from step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that even the חכמים forbid returning the pot when the hole collapsed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the חכמים only meant an intact hole, their ruling is too obvious for anyone to argue. So the dispute must be about a ruined hole, with the חכמים allowing it.

steps.title: The dispute is only about worrying that the hole may be ruined
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is an intact hole. The two sides argue about whether we worry that the hole will get ruined.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really, the case is where the hole was not ruined. Here they argue about whether we worry. One master holds we worry the hole may get ruined, and one master holds we do not worry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב. Everyone agrees a ruined hole is forbidden, and the argument is about a worry, not about an actual ruined hole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה makes you tilt the basket because he worries the hole could collapse when you lift the pot, and then you might put it back anyway. The חכמים do not share this worry, so they allow simply lifting the pot out and putting it back. This removes the 'too obvious' problem, and רב's rule still stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Both the חכמים and רבי אלעזר בן עזריה agree that if the hole collapsed, the pot may not go back. They only argue about whether to worry that it might collapse.

phrases.english: No, really it is where it was not ruined,
and here they disagree about whether we are concerned.
One master holds we are concerned
phrases.notes: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה

phrases.english: that perhaps the hole got ruined,
and the other master holds we are not concerned.
phrases.notes: The חכמים

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, לְעוֹלָם דְּלָא נִתְקַלְקְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines what the dispute is about: an intact hole, with an argument over a precaution.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים allow returning the pot even when the hole was ruined.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone forbids returning the pot to a ruined hole. The dispute is only whether we worry the hole may be ruined.

steps.title: רב הונא on a daffodil branch stuck in earth
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that a daffodil branch in earth may be pulled out on שבת only if, before שבת, it was stuck in, pulled out, and stuck in again.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: this daffodil branch, if he stuck it in, pulled it out, and stuck it in again, it is permitted. If not, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new related rule about pulling an object out of earth on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pulling the branch out of packed earth could move the dirt around it on שבת. If he already stuck it in and pulled it out before שבת, the hole is already loose and wide, so nothing new happens on שבת. Like the pot in step 22, the whole question is whether the hole stays as it is.

keyTerms.meaning: A fragrant daffodil branch kept in moist earth

steps.confusionAlert: Sticking it in, pulling it out, and sticking it in again all happen before שבת. The question is only about pulling it out on שבת itself.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
This daffodil branch:
if he stuck it in, pulled it out,
phrases.notes: Done before שבת.

phrases.english: and then stuck it in again, it is permitted.
phrases.notes: It may be pulled out on שבת.

phrases.english: And if not, it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: הַאי סְלִיקוּסְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related ruling about removing objects from a hole without disturbing what surrounds it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A branch in earth may be pulled out on שבת only if it was inserted, removed, and reinserted before שבת.

steps.title: שמואל on a knife stuck between bricks
steps.stepSummary: שמואל gives the same rule for a knife stored between bricks.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: this knife that is between bricks, if he stuck it in, pulled it out, and stuck it in again, it is permitted. If not, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a second example of the same rule, this time with a knife between bricks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pulling a knife out from tight bricks could loosen the bricks or the material around them on שבת. If he already loosened the space before שבת, pulling it out on שבת changes nothing. So the rule is the same as רב הונא's.
steps.whatToRemember: An object stuck tightly into earth or bricks may be pulled out on שבת only if its space was already loosened before שבת.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
This knife that is between bricks:
if he stuck it in, pulled it out,
and then stuck it in again, it is permitted.
And if not, it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הַאי סַכִּינָא דְּבֵינֵי אוּרְבֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ruling to רב הונא's, applying the same idea to a knife in bricks.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A knife between bricks may be pulled out on שבת only if it was inserted, removed, and reinserted before שבת.

steps.title: A knife stuck among reeds is fine
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא (some say רב אשי) rules that placing a knife among a bunch of reeds is permitted. The special preparation needed for earth or bricks is not required here.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא, and some say רב אשי, said: Sticking a knife in among a bunch of reeds is perfectly fine.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא adds a related ruling. A knife stuck among reeds can be used on שבת without any special preparation before שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא and שמואל required sticking in, pulling out, and sticking in again before שבת, because of earth or brick material. Reeds are different, so no such preparation is needed. Pulling the knife out does not raise the same worry (רש״י: there is no concern that he will scrape off the bark, which would be the forbidden act of smoothing).

keyTerms.meaning: a bunch or hedge of reeds

phrases.aramaic: מָר זוּטְרָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra, and some say Rav Ashi, said:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is unsure which of the two said it.

phrases.english: Among a bunch of reeds,
phrases.notes: That is, sticking a knife in between the reeds.

phrases.english: it is perfectly fine.
phrases.notes: No preparation before שבת is needed.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר זוּטְרָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a case where the requirement of רב הונא and שמואל does not apply.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A knife placed among reeds may be removed on שבת with no prior preparation.

steps.title: A strong challenge from the turnip under the vine
steps.stepSummary: רב מרדכי tells רבא that רב קטינא raised a strong refutation against רב הונא and שמואל. It comes from a משנה about someone who hides a turnip or radish in the ground under a vine with some leaves showing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרדכי said to רבא: רב קטינא raised a strong refutation. We learned: One who hides turnips or radishes under a vine, if some of their leaves were showing, he does not need to worry...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge to רב הונא and שמואל. It begins quoting a משנה, and the quote continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word תיובתא means a very strong refutation, not just a question. In the משנה, the turnip is simply buried in earth. It does not mention any sticking in and pulling out before שבת. The rest of the משנה (coming next) will allow pulling it out on שבת even though earth moves, which seems to contradict רב הונא and שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: one who hides or buries something (for storage)
he does not need to worry

steps.confusionAlert: The quote is not finished here. 'He does not need to worry' leads into a list (כלאים, שביעית, מעשר, and taking it out on שבת) that comes in the next part of the text. The punch of the challenge is the שבת part.

phrases.english: Rav Mordekhai said to Rava:
phrases.notes: He is reporting someone else's objection.

phrases.english: Rav Ketina raised a strong refutation:
phrases.notes: It is aimed at רב הונא and שמואל.

phrases.english: One who hides turnips and radishes
phrases.notes: He buries them in the ground to store them.

phrases.english: under a grapevine,
phrases.notes: This is why the issue of כלאים will come up.

phrases.english: if some of its leaves were showing,
phrases.notes: So he can grab and pull it out.

phrases.english: he does not need to worry
phrases.notes: The list of what he need not worry about continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב מָרְדֳּכַי לְרָבָא, מֵתִיב רַב קַטִּינָא תְּיוּבְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from adding rulings to attacking the rule of רב הונא and שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule of רב הונא and שמואל that an item stuck in earth needs prior loosening before שבת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה allows pulling a buried turnip out on שבת with no mention of prior loosening, even though earth gets moved.
